title: Relational algebra: from questions to plans
lead: A compact expression can describe an entire query, but every operator needs a clear schema and semantics.
goals: Evaluate relational operators on small datasets
Distinguish set projection from SQL bag projection
Turn a join question into an expression you can check

sections.title: The conceptual framework
sections.html:
To answer “which products cost more than 25?”, we can combine a products table with a prices table, retain qualifying rows, and select the columns we need. Relational algebra (RA) gives names to operations like these. Each operator takes relations, table-shaped collections, and returns a relation, so one step’s result can become the next step’s input.

The lecture connects calculus, algebra, and query plans. The basic operations are selection, which retains rows; projection, which retains columns; rename; union; difference; and product, which combines every pair of rows. Intersection and joins can be built from them. Pure RA uses set semantics and does not retain duplicates. SQL normally uses bag semantics and can retain duplicates. The final slides also list aggregation, duplicate elimination, assignment, sorting, and division.

Closed operators, types and safe calculus

Relational algebra operators produce relations that can feed further operators. That closure has typing conditions: selection preserves a relation schema, projection constructs a selected schema, and product combines attributes with unambiguous names. Referring to a missing attribute is an invalid expression, not a special empty result.

Algebra specifies transformations; relational calculus specifies conditions. Codd-style equivalence concerns safe or domain-independent relational queries, not every unrestricted formula producing a finite result and not every feature of modern SQL. A logical rewrite and a physical algorithm must preserve the intended values and multiplicities under the stated set or bag semantics.

sections.title: An original example: rows, columns, and joins
sections.html:
The example has two tables. R(pid,category) stores product identifiers and categories; S(pid,price) stores product identifiers and prices:

R(pid, category)
(11, tea)
(12, tea)
(13, cake)

S(pid, price)
(11, 20)
(13, 35)
(14, 50)

Keep the category column. Read R’s three rows and remove pid. The intermediate values are tea, tea, cake. The first two rows had different identifiers, but removing those identifiers makes both rows tea. Because a pure RA result is a set, retain one copy of each row: the final result is {tea,cake}.

Key takeaway

Projection in pure RA removes duplicate rows after selecting columns. R has no fully identical rows, but removing pid can make two rows identical. SQL SELECT category retains tea, tea, cake; SELECT DISTINCT category removes duplicates.

Only now introduce the notation: π category(R) = {tea,cake}. Read this as “project the category column from R”. The symbol π denotes projection, category specifies the column, and R is the input. Compare PDF pages 7–9 on set semantics, selection, and projection.

  • Keep qualifying rows. Examine each R row’s category and retain only tea: {(11,tea),(12,tea)}. Write σ category=tea(R); σ denotes selection, and its condition determines which rows survive.
  • Combine every pair. Each R row combines with all three S rows, producing 3×3=9 tuples, including pairs whose identifiers do not match. Write R × S.
  • Keep only pairs with the same pid. Among the nine pairs, only identifiers 11 and 13 match. The theta join R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid S returns columns (R.pid,category,S.pid,price) with rows (11,tea,11,20), (13,cake,13,35).
  • Return the required columns. Remove both pid columns from the join result to obtain {(tea,20),(cake,35)}. Write π category,price(R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid S).

Distinguish R.pid from S.pid in a theta join, a join with an explicit condition. A natural join automatically compares every shared column name, so adding a same-named column to both tables can change its join condition.

Renaming gives a self-join two roles

Rename Employee as E and a second occurrence as M. The relationship E.manager_id = M.id matches an employee to that employee's manager. E.id = M.id would match an employee to the same identifier instead. Renaming disambiguates relation/attribute roles; it does not itself change tuple values or cardinality.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 13, 16, 17 ↗. The worked examples are original.

Natural join and the wider operator vocabulary

A natural join uses all shared attribute names and keeps one copy of each shared attribute. R(pid, category) and S(pid, price) produce (pid, category, price). A theta join with an explicit equality can retain both input key attributes before projection. If no attribute names are shared, natural join becomes a Cartesian product.

Extended operator names describe additional tasks: gamma groups and aggregates, delta removes bag duplicates, assignment names an intermediate result, tau orders a result, and division captures an all-required-values condition. The slide deck names these operators; the following division exercise is original explanatory practice rather than a reconstructed slide proof.

Source topics: Physical PDF pp. 10, 11, 14, 15, 18, 19 ↗. The worked examples are original.

sections.title: Two plans, one result: a data-based proof
sections.html:
We want the categories of products with price > 25. Plan A: join R and S first, obtaining product 11 at price 20 and product 13 at price 35; the price filter keeps product 13. Plan B: filter S first, obtaining (13,35) and (14,50); joining with R keeps only identifier 13 because R has no identifier 14. Both plans then project category and return {cake}.

Expression A: π category(σ price>25(R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid S)). Expression B: π category(R ⋈ R.pid=S.pid σ price>25(S)). Read from the innermost operation outwards: input → join/filter → select columns. A produces two join rows and filters them down to one; B first filters S down to two rows and then produces one join row.

Additional reasoning. The predicate, or filter condition, uses only S.price. Every S row with price ≤ 25 will be rejected regardless of the R row it joins with, so the condition can be checked early.

Key takeaway

Push a condition only into an input containing every column it needs. If the condition needs both R and S, S alone lacks enough information to evaluate it. This argument applies to the example’s inner join; it must not be transferred unchanged to an outer join.

This exercise practises proving that two plans are equivalent. Detailed optimisation rules appear in later lectures.

sections.title: Set exercises and self-check
sections.html:
Let A(x)={1,2,4} and B(x)={2,3}. Compute their union, difference, and intersection before revealing the answer.

Answer

A∪B={1,2,3,4}; A−B={1,4}; A∩B={2}; A−(A−B)={2}. If two schemas have incompatible column counts or types, adjust the schemas before applying these set operations.

A deeper question: must π category(R) contain fewer rows than R? No. If all three categories are different, the row count stays unchanged. EXCEPT ALL is only named in the deck; a formula for each row’s multiplicity is not developed here.

Division and bag difference: count the requirement precisely

Skill contains (An, SQL), (An, RA), (Binh, SQL); Required contains SQL and RA. Skill divided by Required returns An because An has every required skill. Binh lacks RA. Under set semantics, use the candidate domain π_person(Skill); if Required is empty, every candidate in that domain satisfies the condition. This formulation assumes ordinary set values, not SQL NULL.

For a tuple appearing three times on the left and once on the right, EXCEPT ALL returns max(3 − 1, 0) = 2 copies. Distinct EXCEPT returns no copy of that tuple because it occurs on the right. The SQLite engine does not support EXCEPT ALL; the Relational Lab models bag difference separately.

Exercise: add (Binh, RA). Who now satisfies the division?

Worked answer. An and Binh. The required set is unchanged, and both candidates now cover SQL and RA.

quiz.question: If R has 3 rows and S has 4 rows, how many rows does R × S contain?
quiz.explanation: Each R row combines with every S row: 3×4=12. The Cartesian product has not yet applied a join condition; a later selection may reduce the number of pairs.
